analysis.one_liner: Sets up voluntary public financing, free TV time, and mandatory debates for Senate campaigns, and bans party soft money.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one senator with zero cosponsors, the bill got six committee hearings but never a Senate vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Bill Bradley's bill would have made Senate general elections publicly financed. Candidates who agreed to debates and strict contribution rules would get public payments and hours of free broadcast time instead of raising money from large donors. It would also have shut down 'soft money' — the unlimited contributions that national party committees raised outside normal contribution limits — and required TV and radio stations to give each eligible Senate candidate two hours of free airtime, one in prime time.
analysis.who_benefits: Senate candidates who accept the rules — they get public campaign payments, two hours of free TV and radio time per station in their state, and no longer need to chase large contributions. Voters benefit from seeing Senate campaigns funded by small, disclosed donations and from mandatory candidate debates, plus new public-service announcements on how to register and vote.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and Senate candidates who forgo big donors

how_it_helps.text: Eligible Senate candidates would be barred from accepting contributions for the general election and instead receive payments from a new Senate Election Campaign Fund in the Treasury. [S2] [S3]

To qualify, candidates could not take more than $100 total from any individual for the primary, could take no contributions from corporations, unions, or other entities, and had to agree in writing to participate in at least two debates. [S2] [S3]

Broadcast licensees would have to provide each eligible Senate candidate two hours of free airtime, at least one hour in prime time, in the 90 days before the election, plus equal free time whenever opponents bought independent-expenditure ads. [S2] [S3]

National party committees and any entities they control would be barred from soliciting or accepting 'soft money' — contributions not subject to federal limits or reporting — and any party spending that could affect a federal election would fall under federal limits and disclosure rules. [S2] [S3]
Candidates and federal officeholders would face federal limits and reporting on fundraising for federal elections, and party committees would have to report all receipts and disbursements. [S2] [S3]

Taxpayers could designate between $1 and $5,000 of their income tax to the Senate Election Campaign Fund, and the FEC would run public-service announcements on voter registration and voting requirements. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers who opt in — the fund is filled by a voluntary income-tax designation matched by appropriations. Broadcast stations would give up two hours of paid-advertising inventory per Senate candidate per cycle. Large donors, corporations and unions, and national party committees would lose the current channels of unlimited or loosely limited money into Senate campaigns.
analysis.who_pays_short: Opt-in taxpayers, broadcasters, big donors, parties

drawbacks.text: The public fund depends on voluntary taxpayer designations of $1 to $5,000 on income tax returns, so payments to candidates could be small or uneven from state to state, since each state's share is based on its own taxpayers' donations. [S2] [S3]

The bill mandates free airtime from broadcast licensees, a real cost to stations in lost advertising inventory and one that broadcasters have historically challenged as a government taking of their property. [S3]

Candidates who accept the program face strict spending and contribution limits while independent groups could still spend unlimited money against them, which the bill only partially answers by granting equal free response time. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design directly addresses the main complaint about Senate campaigns — the need to raise money from large donors and party soft-money channels — by replacing it with a capped, disclosed, publicly funded alternative plus free airtime and required debates. The main design weaknesses are that funding depends on voluntary checkoffs that may yield modest amounts, and that it does nothing about independent spending by outside groups, leaving a lane for unlimited money that the free-airtime response rule only partly offsets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which held six rounds of hearings on it but never voted to report it, so it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Bradley introduced the Senate Campaign Finance Reform Act of 1996 on January 25, 1996, with no cosponsors. [S1] [S2] [S4]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration. [S5]
The Rules and Administration Committee held hearings on the bill six times between February 1 and May 15, 1996, printing them as S.Hrg. 104-542, but took no further action. [S5]
The bill never received a Senate floor vote and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome preserved the status quo that benefited large donors, corporations and unions, and national party committees' soft-money fundraising — and spared broadcast stations a free-airtime mandate. Senate incumbents who fundraise under those rules faced no new limits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large donors, party soft-money committees, broadcasters

against.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill six times but never reported it out, keeping it off the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: One Democrat sponsored the bill with zero cosponsors and no floor vote ever occurred, so the record shows no roll calls and no measureable party split.

industries.note: The bill would have required every licensee in a Senate state to give each eligible candidate two hours of free airtime, one hour in prime time, plus equal free time responding to opposition independent ads — paid inventory given away. The public interest in hearing candidates at length ran directly against the stations' interest in selling that time.

The bill bans national party committees from soliciting or accepting soft money — unlimited, loosely regulated contributions — and subjects party spending that could affect federal elections to federal limits and disclosure. Parties would lose their largest unregulated fundraising channel.

Candidates joining the program could accept no entity contributions and at most $100 per individual for primaries, replacing large-donor funding with public payments. Wealthy contributors and interest groups would lose their main lever over Senate candidates.
Public financing plus mandatory free airtime would shrink the paid-advertising marketplace that Senate campaigns currently fund. Fewer dollars would flow through consultants and stations.
